payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
When a major label signs a licensing deal with an AI music company, its artists at least know who negotiated. Independent artists rarely have that clarity. Their recordings reach the world through intermediaries, and some of those intermediaries can make decisions about a catalog's use that the artist never sees announced.

The question is no longer hypothetical even for signed artists. The American Federation of Musicians has sued Universal and Warner, arguing that licensing members' recordings to AI companies is a new use under the union's recording agreement, and that the musicians who played on those recordings were neither paid nor credited. The labels have moved to dismiss, and the case is unresolved. If that dispute can arise inside a label system with contracts and a union watching, an independent catalog with three or four intermediaries deserves a closer look.

I've spent years working with independent artists and labels across the Americas, and most of them could not say, without looking, what their distributor's terms allow. Before deciding whether to opt in to anything, an independent artist has a prior question to settle: who else might be in a position to say yes on their behalf.

Map everyone who touches the catalog

List every party that holds your recordings or represents your compositions. For most independents that means a distributor, and sometimes a label services company, an independent-label collective that licenses on its members' behalf, a publishing administrator, and the societies that collect performance income.

Each of these has its own agreement with you, and each agreement has its own language about new uses of the catalog. The distributor's terms are usually the place to start, because the distributor is the party delivering your files to the world.

Read the clause about new uses

Most of these agreements were written before generative AI was a commercial question. Look for the clauses that govern licensing to third parties, new technologies, or uses not listed elsewhere in the contract. Broad language there can let an intermediary include your catalog in a deal without asking you first.

Then check the intermediary's notices. When a distributor or collective joins an AI licensing arrangement, the announcement often goes out as an email or a dashboard banner, sometimes with an opt-out window attached. A window that closes while you aren't looking is an answer you gave by default.

If the terms are unclear, ask in writing whether any current or planned agreement allows AI training on your catalog, and how you opt out. Machine-readable reservations exist as well, but the crawlers they address don't reliably read them, so a written answer from a person is the one that holds.

Make your answer the record

Whatever you decide, put it in writing to each party on your list and keep the replies. What you need to hold depends on the answer.

A · Opting out

A confirmation from every door

A dated reply in writing from each intermediary that could have opted you in. One missing reply is one door still open.

B · Opting in

The deal and who signed it

Which arrangement you joined and through whom, since that party is the one who will account for the payments.

Repeat the check whenever you sign with a new distributor or administrator. Terms travel with each agreement, and a catalog that was out under one contract can end up back in under the one that replaces it.

payload.title: Find out who already answered for your catalog
